ta-l1d8q4-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for the second part of Distinction 8, on divine simplicity. Lombard first states his thesis and then proves it from Augustine. He shows the multiplicity of creatures, first bodily and then spiritual (the soul is simple compared with body but manifold in itself), and then God's simplicity, which holds although God is called manifold. He resolves a doubt and excludes all composition from God: specifically the composition of accident and subject, from which he concludes that God is not even properly called substance, and universally any composition, since there is nothing in the divine essence that is not that essence. Thomas announces two inquiries, on divine and on creaturely simplicity. The first has three articles: whether God is wholly simple, whether he is in the category of substance, and whether the other categories are said of him.
claims: God alone is properly and truly simple; creatures, bodily and spiritual, are manifold.
There is nothing in the divine essence that is not the essence itself.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e133.summary: First objection that God is not wholly simple. Being to which no addition is made is common being, predicated of all things and of which nothing can be denied. God is not such, so something is added to his being.
claims: Being without addition is common being.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e136.summary: Second objection from Boethius: whatever exists participates being in order to be, and something else in order to be something. God most truly is and is something, being good and wise, so he has his being and something further by which he is something.
claims: Boethius distinguishes that by which a thing is from that by which it is something.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e142.summary: Third objection. Whatever has something predicated of it that is not of its substance is not simple. What begins to be predicated of something is not of its substance, since nothing's substance comes to it anew. 'Lord' and 'Creator' are predicated of God from time, so God is not simple.
claims: What is newly predicated is not of the substance.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e146.summary: Fourth objection. Wherever several things are in one there is some composition, and in the divine nature three really distinct persons agree in one essence.
claims: Several things in one implies composition.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e149.summary: Sed contra. Every composite is posterior to its components, since the simpler is first in itself before something is added to compose a third. Nothing is prior to the first simply, and God is the first principle.
claims: Every composite is posterior to its components.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e152.summary: Second sed contra. The first giver of being to all has being independent of another, since what depends on another has its being from another. The being of every composite depends on its components, without which it is removed in reality and in thought. So God is not composite.
claims: The first giver of being has independent being.
A composite's being depends on its components.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e155.summary: Third sed contra. The first principle of being has being in the noblest way, since the cause is always nobler than the effect. The noblest way of having being is that the whole thing is its own being, so God is his being. No composite is wholly its being, since its being follows components that are not being itself. So God is not composite, which is to be granted simply.
claims: The noblest mode of having being is to be one's own being.
God is his own being and therefore not composite.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e158.summary: Reply to the first objection. Something is 'without addition' in two ways. It may belong to its concept that nothing is added to it, and this is said of God. Such a being must be perfect in itself, since it receives no addition, and cannot be common, since everything common is realized in the proper, where addition occurs. Or it may belong to its concept neither that addition is made nor that it is not, and this is how common being is 'without addition'. Its concept does not include the condition 'without addition', or it could never receive any, so it can be determined to the proper. Similarly 'animal' in general is without reason in the sense of not including it, while 'donkey' is without reason by including its negation, which determines it to its proper difference. So divine being is determined in itself and divided from all else precisely because no addition can be made to it, and negations said of God imply no composition.
claims: Divine being is 'without addition' by its very concept; common being is so only by not including addition.
Divine being is individuated and distinguished from all else precisely by excluding addition.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e161.summary: Reply to the second objection. In creatures a thing is determined to be something in three ways: by adding a difference potentially in the genus, by a common nature being received in something so as to become this, or by an added accident (knowing, white). None applies to God. He is not something common, since it belongs to his concept that nothing is added; his nature is not received in anything, since he is pure act; and he receives nothing beyond his essence, which contains all perfection. He is determined by negating all addition of himself. By his absolute being he not only is but is something, and in him 'that by which he is' and 'being something' differ only in mode of signifying or concept. Boethius speaks of what participates being, not of God, who is his being essentially. So the attributes make no composition: wisdom composes not by its concept but by its being as really distinct from a subject, which does not hold in God.
claims: Creatures are determined by difference, by reception in a subject, or by accident; none applies to God.
By his absolute being God both is and is something.
Attributes cause composition only when really distinct from their subject, which is not so in God.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e165.summary: Reply to the third objection. Relations said of God from time posit nothing really in him but only in the creature. As the Philosopher says, something is said relatively not because it is related but because something is related to it, as in all cases where one depends on another and not conversely. The knowable is relative only because knowledge is related to it; the knowable does not depend on knowledge, but the reverse. Because our intellect cannot grasp a relation in one extreme without understanding it in the other, it posits a relation in the knowable and signifies it relatively, but the relation is only conceptual in the knowable and real in the knowledge. Likewise the relation implied by 'Lord' or 'Creator' posits something in God only in our understanding, really only in the creature. So the diversity of God's relations to creatures causes no composition in him.
claims: Temporal relations of God to creatures are real in creatures and only conceptual in God.
A thing can be denominated relatively because another is related to it, as the knowable is to knowledge.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e168.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. As shown in Distinction 2, the personal property compared to the essence does not differ from it really and so does not compose with it. Compared to its correlative it makes a real distinction, but on that side there is no union and so no composition. Three things are there, then, without any composition, and personal names signify no composition in God.
claims: Personal properties are really identical with the essence and really distinct only from their correlatives, so they imply no composition.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e180.summary: First argument that God is in the category of substance. Everything is substance or accident, and God is not an accident, so he is substance. Substance is predicated of him substantially and not conversely, since not every substance is God, so it is predicated of him as a genus.
claims: Everything is either substance or accident.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e183.summary: Second argument. Substance is what is not in a subject but is a being through itself, and this belongs to God most of all.
claims: Substance is a being per se, not in a subject.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e186.summary: Third argument. Everything is measured by the least in its genus (the Philosopher), and the Commentator says that what all substances are measured by is the first mover, God. So God is in the genus of substance.
claims: Each genus is measured by its first and least member.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e190.summary: Sed contra. Whatever is in the genus of substance is either the most general genus or contained under it. God is not the most general genus, since then he would be predicated of all substances, nor contained under it, since he would add something to the genus and would not be supremely simple.
claims: God is neither the supreme genus of substance nor contained under it.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e193.summary: Second sed contra and Thomas's determination. Whatever is in a genus has being determined to it, but divine being is determined to no genus and contains the nobilities of all (the Philosopher and the Commentator). So God is not in the genus of substance, and this is to be granted simply. Four reasons are given. (1) From the name: 'substance' is imposed from standing under (substando), and God stands under nothing. (2) Whatever is in a genus adds something to the genus, so the supremely simple cannot be in one. (3) Avicenna's subtler reason: whatever is in a genus has a quiddity distinct from its being, as humanity can be understood while not knowing whether any man exists. Genus and species are predicated in quid and signify a quiddity that has being only as received in this or that, so they are shared by one common concept, not one being. In God being is his quiddity, otherwise it would be accidental to the quiddity and acquired from another, so God cannot be in any genus. (4) From the perfection of divine being, which gathers the nobilities of all genera and so is determined to none.
claims: God is not in the genus of substance or any genus.
Whatever is in a genus has a quiddity distinct from its being; in God being is his quiddity.
Divine being contains the perfections of all genera and is determined to none.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e196.summary: Reply to the first argument. God is simply not an accident, but he cannot quite properly be called substance either, both because the name comes from standing under and because substance names a quiddity distinct from its being. The division into substance and accident is a division of created being. Loosely, God can be called substance, understood as above all created substance with respect to its perfections, such as not being in another. Then predicate and subject are the same, as in all divine predication, and it does not follow that every substance is God, since nothing else receives 'substance' in this sense. Because of this different mode of predicating, 'substance' is said of God and creatures analogically, not univocally. This is another reason God is in no genus: nothing is predicated univocally of him and others.
claims: The division of being into substance and accident applies to created being.
God may be called substance loosely, analogically, as above all created substance.
Nothing is predicated univocally of God and creatures, so God is in no genus.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e199.summary: Reply to the second argument. According to Avicenna, 'what is not in a subject' cannot be the definition of substance. Being is not a genus, and the negation 'not in a subject' posits nothing, so 'a being not in a subject' does not signify a genus. Every genus must signify a quiddity whose concept does not include being, whereas 'being' signifies not a quiddity but the act of being itself. So it does not follow that what is not in a subject is in the genus of substance, and that definition in any case does not fit God.
claims: 'Being not in a subject' does not define substance, since being is not a genus.
A genus signifies a quiddity whose concept excludes being.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e202.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Measure' properly belongs to quantity, as that by which a quantity is known: the least in the genus, either simply, as unity in numbers, or by convention, as a palm for cloth or a stadium for roads, in continua that have no simple minimum. The name is transferred to every genus, so the first, simplest, and most perfect in each is the measure of the rest, by which each is known to have more or less of the genus's truth, as white is among colours. In substance, the one with the most perfect and simplest being, God, is the measure of all substances. So he need not be in the genus as contained but only as principle, having its whole perfection, like unity in numbers but differently. Unity measures only numbers and is contained in a determinate genus as its principle, whereas God measures the perfections of all genera (wisdom, power) and so is not contained in any genus.
claims: The first and most perfect of a genus is its measure.
God is the measure of substances and of all perfections as principle, not as a member of a genus.
concepts: God as measure of all perfections

ta-l1d8q4-d1e214.summary: First argument that the other categories are said of God. Whatever a species is predicated of, its genus is too. Knowledge, a species of quality, and magnitude, a species of quantity, are found in God, so quality and quantity are too.
claims: Whatever has the species has the genus.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e217.summary: Second argument. The Philosopher says that one in substance makes the same, in quantity the equal, in quality the like. Equality and likeness are truly found in God, so something is said of him in the mode of quantity and quality.
claims: Equality presupposes quantity; likeness presupposes quality.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e223.summary: Third argument. The nature of a genus is found most properly in what is first in it, and God is the first agent, so action is found in him above all.
claims: A genus is most properly realized in its first member.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e227.summary: Fourth argument. The weaker a thing's being, the more it conflicts with supreme perfection. Relation has the weakest being of all (the Commentator) and is founded on the others, as equality on quantity. Since relation is found in God, the other categories are found there all the more.
claims: Relation has the weakest being of all categories.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e230.summary: Sed contra from Augustine: whatever is said of God is said either by substance or by relation, so the other categories are not in God; Lombard cites the same authority.
claims: Whatever is said of God is said by substance or by relation.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e236.summary: Thomas's determination. Whatever found in creatures is predicated of God is predicated eminently (Dionysius), so every imperfection must be removed. In each of the nine accidental categories there are two things: the character of accident and the proper character of the genus. The character of accident implies imperfection, since an accident's being is to inhere and depend and so to compose with a subject, and nothing can be predicated of God in that respect. As to the proper character of each genus, every genus other than relation implies imperfection, since it is defined by comparison to the subject: quantity is the measure of substance, quality its disposition, and so on. So these are excluded by their generic character too. Some of their species, however, imply perfection by their completing differences, such as knowledge and virtue, and are predicated of God by the proper character of the species, not of the genus. Relation, even by its generic character, implies no dependence on a subject but is toward something outside, and so it is found in God even by its generic character. Hence only two modes of predication remain in God, by substance and by relation, since modes of predication belong to genera, not species.
claims: Accidents as such cannot be predicated of God, since inherence implies imperfection.
Of the accidental categories, only relation is found in God by its generic character, since it implies no dependence on a subject.
Species such as knowledge are predicated of God by their perfecting difference, not their genus.
Only two modes of predication remain in God: substance and relation.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e239.summary: Reply to the first argument. Knowledge is predicated of God not by the character of its genus but by its proper completing difference, so it is said of God and others not univocally but by priority and posteriority.
claims: Knowledge is said of God by its specific difference, analogically.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e242.summary: Reply to the second argument. Some things in God are said to have the mode of quantity or quality, not because they are predicated of him in that mode but because of the mode in which they are found in creatures, since the names we impose have the mode of quality and quantity. Damascene says some things are said of God as following the substance, though as they are in him nothing follows.
claims: Divine names have the mode of quantity or quality only from their creaturely imposition.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e245.summary: Reply to the third argument. Action as a category means something flowing from the agent with motion, but in God nothing really intervenes between him and his work. So he is not an agent by the action that is a category; his action is his substance (treated more fully in Book II, Dist. 1).
claims: God's action is his substance, not the category of action.

ta-l1d8q4-d1e249.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The weakness of relation's being lies in its inherence in a subject, since it posits nothing absolute in the subject, only a respect to another. For that very reason it is better suited to divine predication: the less it adds, the less it conflicts with simplicity.
claims: Relation suits divine predication because it adds nothing absolute to its subject.

ta-l1d8q4-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 4 maps the second part of Distinction 8, on divine simplicity: the multiplicity of bodily and spiritual creatures, the simplicity of God, and the exclusion from him of accidental and every other composition. It announces inquiries into divine and creaturely simplicity.

ta-l1d8q4-Dd1e125.summary: Article 1 asks whether God is wholly simple. The sed contra arguments prove that the first principle is not composite, since a composite is posterior to and dependent on its components, and the first principle has being in the noblest way, by being its own being. The replies distinguish God's being, 'without addition' by its concept and so determined and distinct, from common being, 'without addition' only by not including it. They show that God is determined neither by difference, nor by reception, nor by accident, and that his attributes, his temporal relations (real only in creatures), and the personal properties (really identical with the essence) imply no composition.
claims: God is wholly simple, being his own being.
Divine being, unlike common being, excludes addition by its very concept.
Temporal relations and personal properties imply no composition in God.

ta-l1d8q4-Dd1e172.summary: Article 2 asks whether God is in the category of substance. Thomas holds that he is in no genus, for four reasons: the name 'substance' (from standing under), the addition that belongs to whatever is in a genus, Avicenna's argument that whatever is in a genus has a quiddity distinct from its being, and the perfection of divine being. God may be called substance only loosely and analogically. 'Being not in a subject' does not define substance, since being is not a genus, and God is the measure of all genera as principle, not as member.
claims: God is not in the genus of substance or any genus.
In God being is his quiddity, which excludes membership in a genus.
Substance is said of God and creatures analogically.

ta-l1d8q4-Dd1e206.summary: Article 3 asks whether the other categories are said of God. Thomas holds that the character of accident, inherence and dependence, excludes all accidental categories as such. Of their generic characters, all but relation imply comparison to a subject. Relation, which implies only a respect to another, is found in God by its generic character, while perfect species such as knowledge are predicated by their completing difference, analogically. So only two modes of divine predication remain, by substance and by relation. God's action is his substance, and relation suits God because it adds nothing absolute.
claims: Only substance and relation remain as modes of predication in God.
Relation alone among accidents is found in God by its generic character.

ta-l1d8q4.summary: Quaestio 4 of Book I, Distinction 8 treats divine simplicity. Article 1 proves that God is wholly simple, being his own being. It distinguishes divine being, which by concept excludes addition and is thereby distinct from all else, from common being, which merely abstracts from addition. It also shows that attributes, temporal relations (real only in creatures), and personal properties introduce no composition. Article 2 denies that God is in the genus of substance or any genus, chiefly because whatever is in a genus has a quiddity distinct from its being, whereas God's being is his quiddity. 'Substance' is said of him only analogically, and he is the measure of all genera as principle. Article 3 holds that the accidental categories are excluded from God as accidents. Relation alone is found in God by its generic character, and perfect species such as knowledge are predicated analogically, so only substance and relation remain as modes of divine predication.
claims: God is wholly simple: he is his own being, without composition of any kind.
God is in no genus, since his being is his quiddity.
Only substance and relation remain as modes of predication in God.
